explain: _satis_ (enough) is followed by the genitive of the thing there is enough of: _aquae_ is the genitive singular of _aqua_.
distractors: _aquam_ is accusative. After _satis_ the thing measured goes in the genitive: _aquae_.
_aqua_ is nominative (or ablative). After _satis_ you need the genitive: _aquae_.
_aquārum_ is genitive plural (“of waters”). One portion of water is singular: _aquae_.

en: I drink a lot of wine.
explain: _multum_ (much) is a quantity, so the wine is genitive: _vīnī_ (genitive of _vīnum_). _multum_ itself never changes.
distractors: _vīnum_ is nominative or accusative. After _multum_ the thing measured is genitive: _vīnī_.
_vīnō_ is dative or ablative. After _multum_ you need the genitive: _vīnī_.
_vīnōrum_ is genitive plural (“of wines”). Wine as a drink is singular: _vīnī_.

explain: _parum_ (too little, not enough) works like _satis_ and _multum_: the food is genitive, _cibī_.
distractors: _cibō_ is dative or ablative. After _parum_: genitive, _cibī_.
_cibōrum_ is genitive plural (“of foods”). Food as a mass is singular: _cibī_.

explain: _paulum_ (a little) is followed by the genitive of what there is a little of: _pecūniae_.
distractors: _pecūnia_ is nominative or ablative. After _paulum_: genitive, _pecūniae_.
_pecūniārum_ is genitive plural (“of monies”). Money as a mass is singular: _pecūniae_.

explain: Negative or positive, _multum_ takes the genitive: _multum pecūniae_. _nōn_ goes before the verb.
distractors: _pecūnia_ is nominative or ablative. After _multum_: genitive, _pecūniae_.
_pecūniārum_ is genitive plural. Money as a mass is singular: _pecūniae_.

en: How much wine do you drink?
explain: _quantum_ (how much) asks about an amount, so the thing is genitive: _quantum vīnī_ is “how much (of) wine”.
distractors: _vīnum_ is nominative or accusative. After _quantum_: genitive, _vīnī_.
_vīnō_ is dative or ablative. After _quantum_: genitive, _vīnī_.
_vīnōrum_ is genitive plural. Wine as a drink is singular: _vīnī_.

explain: _plūs_ (more) is a quantity word like _satis_: the water is genitive, _aquae_.
distractors: _aqua_ is nominative or ablative. After _plūs_: genitive, _aquae_.
_aquārum_ is genitive plural (“of waters”). Water as a mass is singular: _aquae_.

en: We have enough food and wine.
explain: Both things depend on _satis_, so both are genitive: _cibī et vīnī_.
distractors: Both nouns are accusative here. Both depend on _satis_, so both are genitive: _cibī et vīnī_.
_cibī_ is right, but _vīnum_ is not: both nouns depend on _satis_, so _vīnī_ too.
_cibō_ and _vīnō_ are dative or ablative. After _satis_: genitive, _cibī et vīnī_.

explain: _nihil_ (nothing) is followed by the genitive: “nothing of new”. _novī_ is the genitive of _novum_ (a new thing).
distractors: _novō_ is dative or ablative. The thing there is nothing of goes in the genitive: _novī_.
_novōrum_ is genitive plural (“of new things”). The saying uses the singular: _nihil novī_.

explain: Literally “what of new?”. _quid_ (what) is followed by a genitive, just as _nihil_ and _satis_ are. The answer is _Nihil novī_ (nothing new).
distractors: _novō_ is dative or ablative. The “of new” is genitive: _novī_.
_novōrum_ is genitive plural. The question uses the singular: _quid novī_.
